title: Zelenskyy says Trump approved Patriot production licenses for Ukraine as Kyiv confronts interceptor shortages and escalating Russian strikes
body: “There are concrete agreements regarding Patriot licenses,” Zelenskyy posted online. “At our meeting, President Trump stressed that he had made his final decision: Ukraine will receive licenses to produce Patriot missiles.” Ukraine has repeatedly asked Washington for domestic Patriot production rights to strengthen its air defenses. Zelenskyy told CNN in August that Ukraine had only 10 percent of the interceptor missiles required to counter Russian attacks. Russian forces have recently intensified strikes on Ukraine’s power grid using ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones. The attacks come ahead of the winter season. President Trump and I had a meeting where we discussed general matters. After that, our negotiating teams held a separate, long meeting. The agreement is as follows: we will brief the European side and discuss these details with them; the Americans will speak with the Russians;… — Volodymyr Zelenskyy / Володимир Зеленський (@ZelenskyyUa) September 25, 2026 Patriot interceptors can take more than two years to manufacture because of their technical complexity. The article said supplies were also strained by the U.S.-Israeli war in Iran. Trump said during a NATO summit in Turkey in July that the United States would allow Ukraine to co-produce Patriot missiles. The effort appeared to stall shortly afterward. Zelenskyy later said Ukraine was considering work with U.S. defense contractors to reconfigure Ukrainian-made ballistic missiles as Patriot interceptors. The proposal followed meetings with representatives of Lockheed Martin and Raytheon in Washington. Zelenskyy also said the Trump administration had proposed trilateral talks involving the United States, Ukraine and Russia. The United Arab Emirates was suggested as the venue, but Moscow had made no commitment to participate. “We will brief the European side and discuss these details with them, the Americans will talk to the Russians, and in 10 days’ time we will return with a particular perspective and a result,” Zelenskyy told reporters. The proposal calls for separate consultations between Ukraine and its European partners and between Washington and Moscow. Source: The Hill .

title: Marines Rushing To Equip Amphibious Combat Vehicles With New Anti-Drone Jammers
body: The U.S. Marine Corps is buying Anduril Pulsar-L electronic warfare jammers to meet an urgent operational need to better protect its 8×8 wheeled Amphibious Combat Vehicles (ACV) from drones. This is part of broader efforts the service is pursuing to boost the ACV’s defenses against uncrewed aerial attackers, as well as incoming anti-tank guided missiles and other threats . Drone threats are real now and have notably sidelined even the most advanced heavy armor in Ukraine. Marine Corps Systems Command (MARCORSYSCOM) announced it had awarded a sole-source deal to Anduril, valued at $15,711,445.50, for an unspecified number of Pulsar-Ls, yesterday. This follows a statement of intent the Command put out last month. Anduril first unveiled Pulsar-L , a lightweight addition to its larger Pulsar family of electronic warfare systems , in April 2025. The Marine Corps had 150 baseline personnel carrier variants of the ACV (or ACV-Ps), as well as 21 command-and-control ACV-C versions, in inventory as of April 2026. The default armament for ACV-P currently is just a single .50 caliber M2 machine gun in a remote weapon station on top of the hull. The service’s goal is to eventually acquire 389 ACV-Ps and 33 ACV-Cs, as well as 152 ACV-30s with new 30mm cannon-armed turrets and 34 ACV-R armored recovery vehicle variants. The ACV family has already supplanted the Marine Corps’ previous fleet of tracked Assault Amphibious Vehicles (AAV). From left to right, an Amphibious Combat Vehicle command and control variant (ACV-C), a 30mm cannon-armed ACV-30, and a standard ACV personnel carrier version (ACV-P). The ACV-R recovery variant is not shown here. USMC/Sgt. Alexis Sanchez “The Anduril Pulsar-L system is a platform-integrated omni-directional SK C-UAS [soft-kill counter-uncrewed aerial systems] with a combined sensor/jammer package that detects, tracks, identifies, and defeats radio frequency-dependent Group 1 and Group 2 Unmanned Aerial Systems (UASs),” MARCORSYSCOM wrote in a justification for the sole-source contract, which was also released yesterday. “Additionally, the system provides counter positioning, navigation, and timing capabilities.” The U.S. military definition of a Group 1 drone is any design weighing up to 20 pounds, that is able to fly up to an altitude of 1,200 feet, and that can reach speeds of up to 100 knots. Group 2 is the next tier up, encompassing types with gross weights between 21 and 55 pounds, that can get up to an altitude of 3,500 feet, and hit top speeds of up to 250 knots. Kamikaze drones and other small weaponized types that fall into Groups 1 and 2 are used on a daily basis in Ukraine to attack armored vehicles , as well as unarmored vehicles and personnel . These are threats that have been steadily expanding to other hotspots globally, and that we will come back to later on. Furthermore, “the Pulsar-L is the only solution capable of being mounted on the ACV to provide a mobile and organic means to effectively and simultaneously execute the entire kill-chain against hostile UASs in the deployed land and maritime/littoral environment while not exceeding the limited ACV space, weight, and power claim allotted to the SK C-UAS solution,” according to MARCORSYSCOM. “This will provide the ACV with an essential defensive capability, directly contributing to increased survivability and force protection while not sacrificing the mobility and operational tempo of the ACV.” A row of Marine ACVs seen during training. USMC Pulsar-L is already “in use by the Special Operations Command due to the system’s low weight, proven performance in engaging multiple UASs, and simultaneous execution of the full kill-chain while static or on the move,” the justification document adds. “Additionally, it is the only known commercially available system that meets the minimum requirement to rapidly identify and respond to emerging UAS technologies and tactics without frequent updates to predefined threat data libraries. The Pulsar-L is the only solution that uses machine based learning to continually adapt to these ever-changing threats without requiring vendor updates, allowing the warfighters to continually be effective in the fight.” The latter point here is a particularly important consideration for electronic warfare systems, in general, which need to be able to accurately detect, categorize, and respond to different waveforms to be most effective. The emergence of new waveforms, as well as changes to how existing ones are emitted, together with new tactics, techniques, and procedures, can all negatively impact a system’s performance. Historically, the process of responding to those developments with updates to built-in threat libraries has been lengthy and complex. The conflict in Ukraine has shown that the cycle of new developments in the electromagnetic spectrum and then the need for new countermeasures can be regularly measured in weeks . The U.S. military has been heavily investing in so-called cognitive electronic warfare capabilities to help automate and otherwise accelerate various aspects of this process. The ability of a particular electronic warfare suite to adapt autonomously in real-time, even in the middle of operations, has been viewed as the absolute ‘holy grail’ of this concept, which you can read more about here . How exactly Pulsar-L leverages machine-learning and artificial intelligence to this end, and the speed with which it can adapt to changing threats, is still not entirely clear. Regardless, “there is an unusual and compelling need for the rapid deployment of SK C-UASs to forward-deployed ground units as Marines currently lack the ability to conduct self-defense against emerging UAS threats,” the justification document stresses. “Failure to deliver this capability places Marines at unnecessary risk, potentially leading to mission failure and loss of life, and hampers the Government’s ability to keep them safe during forward deployments.” MARCORSYSCOM’s justification for the sole-source deal to Anduril does not otherwise elaborate on the urgent requirements that drove the deal, which it says were only formalized on April 7. That is notably roughly a week after the United States and Israel first launched major combat operations against Iran , which is a prolific developer and user of various tiers of weaponized drones . There is no explicit confirmation of any link, but Iranian drones, as well as missiles and other capabilities , have been a real threat to U.S. forces in the region. We have also just gained more insights recently into how forward-deployed Marine Corps elements contributed to those operations. Counter-drone capabilities would also be especially critical in any future amphibious landing operation, wherever it might occur. Marines prepare to load an M142 High Mobility Artillery Rocket System (HIMARS) onto a KC-130J aircraft somewhere in the Middle East in July 2026. USAF All that being said, threats posed by armed Group 1 and 2 drones are not at all limited to Iran and the Middle East, nor are they new. They are only likely to become a more ubiquitous feature in the hands of nation-state armed forces and non-state actors in conflict zones globally as time goes on. The nature of these threats is also expanding significantly in scale and scope, especially when it comes to more automated targeting capabilities , thanks heavily to the increasing democratization of AI-driven technologies, something TWZ has explored in depth in the past . A number of other significant developments in this arena have emerged from the conflict in Ukraine, where electronic warfare systems are heavily employed against drones. This includes the introduction of physical fiber-optic control links that cannot be jammed , as well as the use of mesh-like and often ad-hoc networks to increase resiliency. The fighting in Ukraine has also underscored the threat that even small kamikaze drones pose to armored vehicles, including types that are far more heavily protected to start with than the Marine Corps’ ACVs. As mentioned, Ukrainian forces have been sidelining their M1 Abrams and other main battle tanks in the face of constant drone attacks. MARCORSYSCOM’s justification for the Pulsar-L order makes clear that this is just one part of a larger plan to boost the ACV’s defenses. “Marine Corps program of record for SK C-UAS is planned to initiate in FY27,” the document mentions toward the very end. “The components of this future program will be procured through full and open competition as it is expected that advanced non-kinetic and SK defeat technologies should be mature by this time.” Another look at a Marine Corps ACV-P, showing the general configuration of these vehicles today. USMC Marine Corps officials have also talked in the past about integrating active protection systems (APS) , which could be blended together with C-UAS capabilities , and other defensive features to the service’s ACV fleet. “We’re constantly looking at what the next generation of APS is and how we can get that onto the [ACV] platform in a lightweight form factor,” Chris Melkonian, the Marine Corps’ Program Manager for Advanced Amphibious Assault (PM AAA), told TWZ and other attendees at the annual Modern Day Marine exposition in April. Improved “situational awareness, that’s kind of a gateway to counter-UAS, in terms of the ability to sense your environment,” Melkonian also highlighted at that time. “Take all that video on board and then be able to feed that into [a] counter-UAS system.” Additional “overhead protection right now is a critical thing that we’re working on right now for this platform,” he added. The practice of adding on anti-drone armor screens on armored vehicles (and now other platforms ), especially to protect against top-down attacks, first emerged in Russia in the lead-up to the all-out invasion of Ukraine in 2022. However, the installation of this kind of so-called ‘cope cage’ type armor has now become a global trend, including in the U.S. military . The U.S. Marine Corps is also pressing ahead with a larger vision to field several tiers of counter-drone capabilities at all levels of its forces , to better protect everything from static installations at home and abroad right down to individual squads . When it comes to the Marine Corps ACV fleet, the rush order for Pulsar-Ls is an important new step in boosting those vehicles’ defenses against threats that exist now. At the same time, drones are increasingly calling the role of armored vehicles in future conflicts into question. title: “Killing Ukraine’s internet would take nuclear or chemical weapons”—MiroHost founder whose data center Russia just destroyed
body: (function(w,q){w[q]=w[q]||[];w[q].push(["_mgc.load"])})(window,"_mgq"); Russian drones and missiles struck Kyiv data centers over 23–24 September, knocking out internet and hosting providers. The Digital Transformation Ministry said about 100,000 subscribers lost service, NV Business reported . Russia has widened its air campaign from power plants and warehouses to railways, fuel stations, and now digital infrastructure as it tries to grind down the country's ability to function before another war winter. "You'd have to destroy 70-80% of Kyiv's buildings" MiroHost founder and Internet Invest Group head Oleksandr Olshanskyi told NV Business the attack destroyed his own data center. "Most critically important data and systems have been moved abroad or to the cloud," Olshanskyi said. "If an online store stops working, that's unpleasant but not a tragedy." He called rumors about a full internet blackout or sharp service price hikes baseless. "Destroying all internet in a simple way is impossible—you'd have to use nuclear or chemical weapons or destroy 70-80% of buildings in Kyiv," he said. What Russia hit The strikes damaged a Kyiv data center housing UTELS switching equipment on 23 September. Overnight into 24 September, Russia destroyed equipment of hosting provider CityHost.UA and the data center housing MiroHost. About 95% of MiroHost's clients operate outside Ukraine and were unaffected, he said. Russia also struck the Pavutyna network's data center. Crazy Network said a missile struck Kyiv's central traffic exchange hub, cutting service for its subscribers in Vinnytsia, Kyiv, and Khmelnytskyi Oblast. Providers KIEVNET, Domonet, FAUST, and Etherlink also reported disruptions. Ukraine's telecom regulator NKEK said on 24 September that providers were completing emergency restoration, and Domonet estimated service would return by 21:00 that evening. The 23 September strikes killed two people and injured more than 40, and hit a college building in Kyiv while students were on campus, Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha wrote that evening. Russia targeted major Ukrainian data centers "seeking to disrupt the flow of information," he said. "This is critical civilian infrastructure that ensures people can access life-saving information. It is not a military target." "More sanctions pressure, more missile interceptors are the only way to stop this terror," Sybiha wrote. "These attacks must not become the new normal." Panic, not military gain Olshanskyi said Russia uses these strikes to spread fear, not achieve lasting results. "The enemy's goal is to cause damage, inflame panic, and heighten nervousness," he said. His data center's destruction "will not affect the situation at the front in any way," he said. title: To Secure Arctic, NORTHCOM Builds Closer Ties to Pacific, European Commands
body: U.S. Northern Command plans to sign an agreement with its European and Pacific counterparts to enhance coordination and close security seams in the Arctic, a strategically vital region where all three commands converge, U.S. officials told Air & Space Forces Magazine. NORTHCOM’s Gen. Gregory M. Guillot, U.S. European Command’s Gen. Alexus G. Grynkewich, and U.S. Pacific Command’s Adm. Samuel Paparo will finalize the agreement, which aims to strengthen information sharing and ensure that adversaries cannot exploit the geographic boundaries among the commands. U.S. Northern Command’s long-standing motto, “We have the watch,” has taken on greater urgency in recent years as the potential means to attack the U.S. Arctic region have grown. Today, the command’s geographic focus stretches across Canada, Greenland , and south to Mexico and parts of the Caribbean, and the potential dangers have expanded to include a range of emerging threats, from intelligence-gathering balloons to ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and drones. Guillot, in a September interview with Air & Space Forces Magazine, said the command has managed the growth well. “Over the last couple of years, we’ve received a few new missions with Greenland, the Southern Border, Golden Dome, and the counter-UAS mission, and we’ve been able to evolve and incorporate those into our daily homeland defense operations, I think, seamlessly,” said Guillot, whose responsibilities also include heading the binational U.S.-Canadian North American Aerospace Defense Command, known as NORAD. “The command is growing as the number of threats and the number of avenues of approach that they can use to threaten us increase,” he added of NORTHCOM. The Arctic’s strategic importance has grown as melting polar ice has opened up the region for greater commercial traffic and resource exploitation. Russia, which owns more than half the Arctic coastline, has long projected its military might in the region. More recently, China has sought to assert itself as an Arctic nation, not because it controls territory there but because of its value as a transit venue, shortening the trade routes between China and Europe. China operates research vessels there, including submersibles . “They’re seeking to move themselves forward militarily and become global power projectors, not regional power projectors, and part of that will involve holding us at risk through the Arctic and ensuring that policy in the Arctic reflects their interests,” retired Gen. Glen D. VanHerck, Guillot’s predecessor at NORTHCOM and NORAD, said in an interview. A joint China-Russia bomber patrol in the region, which took off in 2024 from a Russian base, demonstrated closer ties between the two and raised concerns across North America and Europe about their growing cooperation. Canadian CF-18 Hornets joined U.S. F-35A Lightning II and F-16 Fighting Falcon fighters, all from NORAD, to intercept Russian TU-95 and Chinese H-6 bombers in the Alaska Air Defense Identification Zone, July 24, 2024. U.S. Department of Defense Photo “When you see Russia and China cooperating militarily in the Arctic, with a greater capacity arguably than anywhere else on Earth, I think that should give some signals that we should be paying attention to what’s going on in the region,” said Iris Ferguson , who served as deputy assistant secretary of defense for Arctic and global resilience from 2022-2025. Ferguson sees closing the gaps between U.S. military commands that converge in the Arctic region as essential to enhanced security. “There are multiple seams in the Arctic for the United States,” she said. “The one between NORTHCOM and EUCOM is a significant one and is one area that deserves more attention.” NORTHCOM led the drive to formalize an agreement with its fellow combatant commands, working closely with EUCOM and its boss, Grynkewich, who is also NATO’s Supreme Allied Commander Europe, with critical ties to NATO’s Nordic allies. Through NATO, Grynkewich is responsible for defending what NATO dubs the High North, comprising Canada, Finland, Norway, Sweden, Denmark, Iceland, and the U.S. The alliance held multiple large-scale Arctic exercises this past summer, some of which Air & Space Forces Magazine experienced firsthand. NATO’s Arctic Sentry “enhanced vigilance activity” operates in cooperation with NORAD and NORTHCOM, and alliance officials describe that cooperation as at a level not seen in decades. Guillot said the potential threats aren’t limited to America’s largest potential adversaries. “I see the threat to our continent changing not just from Russia and China, but from multiple adversaries,” Guillot said. “The biggest change is that it’s from all avenues of approach instead of just from the north, and it’s with systems that could affect us from further away. So therefore our defense capabilities need to be expanded further from our borders to make sure that we’re defending at the appropriate range.” “What that necessitates is cooperation with EUCOM, PACOM, and SOUTHCOM, where we can exchange information, pictures, intelligence, and even resources to defend further away,” Guillot said. VanHerck applauded efforts to strengthen Arctic security and stop threats before they reach North America. “Homeland defense doesn’t start in the homeland,” VanHerck said. “It starts forward with allies and partners and fellow combat commanders forward. Ideally, you have a posture and a presence and enough domain awareness that you deter those activities before they ever start. And if they’re going to attack, you can defeat those adversaries or capabilities further forward.” The Trump administration has made Arctic security a centerpiece of its foreign policy, pressing to win new concessions for American basing in Greenland, expanding beyond a single Space Force installation to establish two new bases . Demonstrating the critical nature of Greenland to North American security, the administration transferred responsibility for Greenland, a territory of Denmark, to U.S. Northern Command, removing it from U.S. European Command’s area of responsibility. That transfer is far from symbolic. “A lot of exercises and operations that we would normally conduct either unilaterally, or perhaps with Canada through NORAD, we’re now doing with other countries to include Denmark,” Guillot said. A recent exercise with the U.S. and allied nations marked the first time Danish F-35s landed in Greenland. title: Poland’s Anti-Ukrainian Violence Is Part of a Wider Battle for Europe
body: Violence against Ukrainians in Poland is rising just as European support for Kyiv becomes more contested. Across Germany, France, Britain and other European countries, opposition to military aid, sanctions and continued financial support is moving from the political margins towards mainstream debate. The forces driving it differ sharply from country to country, from genuine domestic grievances and war fatigue to nationalist politics and long-standing ideological hostility towards NATO. Running through them is another factor: sustained Russian hybrid activity designed to amplify divisions, weaken support for Ukraine and turn domestic disputes into strategic pressure on Europe. Poland, Ukraine’s principal land gateway to the West, is where the consequences are becoming most visible. In the first months after Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022, Poland became the great European exception. Millions of Ukrainians crossed its border. Polish families opened their homes. Railway stations became improvised relief centres. Municipalities, charities, businesses and ordinary citizens organised assistance on a scale that surprised even Poles themselves. The political consensus was similarly strong. Ukraine’s survival was regarded as a Polish security interest, and Poland became the principal land corridor through which Western military assistance reached the Ukrainian armed forces. The Ukrainian presence is visible everywhere. Even on Polish trains, information videos are shown in Ukrainian. Four years later, something considerably darker has entered Polish public life. During the first six months of 2026, Ukrainian citizens made 180 reports to the Polish police concerning suspected hate crimes, according to figures obtained by Rzeczpospolita . The equivalent full-year totals were 267 in 2024 and 275 in 2025. Even allowing for changes in reporting behaviour, the first-half figure represented an increase of more than 30 per cent from the comparable period a year earlier. Separate police figures analysed by the Polish fact-checking organisation Demagog strengthen the conclusion. Using offence categories that allow comparison with earlier years, police recorded 179 confirmed hate crimes in which Ukrainian citizens were victims during the first half of 2026. Among them were 125 offences under the provision covering public insult or violation of bodily integrity on national or ethnic grounds, and 54 cases involving violence or unlawful threats because of nationality or ethnicity. The numbers are still small relative to a Ukrainian population in Poland of well over a million. But cases are disturbing. In on occasion, two 11-year-old Ukrainian girls travelling on a bus in Bielsko-Biała were subjected to a stream of nationalist abuse by a 54-year-old man, who was subsequently charged with publicly insulting them because of their nationality. In Warsaw in May, three Ukrainian teenagers were attacked on the Świętokrzyski Bridge. A 16-year-old suffered a fractured skull. In Wrocław there have been violent attacks in which prosecutors investigated nationality as a motive. Polish media have reported other assaults after victims were heard speaking Ukrainian. There is also a growing prosecutorial response. Poland created 50 specialised prosecution offices to deal with hate speech and prejudice-motivated crime. Between February and June 2026, 283 prejudice-motivated cases were sent to court, including 220 indictments. The phenomenon has consequently moved beyond anecdote. Poland is experiencing a measurable anti-Ukrainian backlash. The more difficult question is why. From Extraordinary Solidarity to Accumulated Resentment The starting point is the extraordinary character of Poland’s original response. Support for receiving Ukrainian refugees reached 94 per cent immediately after Russia’s full-scale invasion, according to CBOS polling. Such unanimity was always likely to weaken as emergency solidarity became permanent coexistence. By July 2026, CBOS recorded a historic reversal. For the first time in its surveys, more Poles opposed accepting further Ukrainian refugees than supported doing so, 52 per cent against 42 per cent. Fifty-four per cent considered the assistance Poland provided to Ukrainian refugees excessive. The same surveys reveal a more complicated picture than simple xenophobia. Eighty-seven per cent supported linking full access to healthcare benefits to insurance contributions, while 58 per cent opposed removing free collective accommodation from Ukrainian mothers with children over one year old. Polish opinion therefore appears increasingly conditional rather than uniformly hostile. Many voters want Ukrainians treated increasingly like other long-term residents rather than as recipients of an exceptional wartime regime. That distinction matters because Russian propaganda works most effectively when it attaches itself to a real argument. Poland has absorbed a very large population in a short period. Schools, housing markets, health services and local government have had to adjust. Ukrainians compete in labour markets and run businesses. Individual crimes committed by Ukrainians receive considerable media and social-media attention. There are legitimate disputes about welfare eligibility, migration rules and the costs of support. Economic evidence, however, undermines one of the most persistent versions of the anti-Ukrainian narrative, the idea that Ukrainian refugees are principally a financial burden living from Polish benefits. A Deloitte analysis commissioned by UNHCR estimated that Ukrainian refugees generated the equivalent of 2.7 per cent of Polish GDP in 2024, with a high employment rate and no detected adverse effect on overall Polish unemployment or real wages. The political usefulness of the welfare argument therefore extends beyond its economic accuracy. It gives resentment a simple vocabulary: Poles pay, Ukrainians receive. That message travels well online. From Welfare to National Identity A crying woman protesting the Russian invasion in the Ukraine. In Krakow, 2022. (Image: Shutterstock) The deeper source of anti-Ukrainian politics lies elsewhere. Poland and Ukraine carry an extraordinarily difficult twentieth-century history, above all the massacres of Polish civilians in Volhynia and Eastern Galicia in 1943 and 1944 by the Ukrainian Insurgent Army, UPA, and other Ukrainian nationalist formations. Tens of thousands of Polish civilians were killed. Those events have not been forgotten in Poland. Contemporary Ukraine’s treatment of the Organisation of Ukrainian Nationalists, the UPA and figures such as Stepan Bandera has repeatedly caused political conflict with Warsaw. That conflict intensified dramatically in 2026 after the naming of a Ukrainian military formation after the Heroes of the UPA. President Karol Nawrocki subsequently stripped Volodymyr Zelenskyy of Poland’s Order of the White Eagle. The row created ideal conditions for politicians who had already moved Ukraine from foreign policy into Poland’s domestic culture wars. The result is visible in opinion research. In July, 46 per cent of Poles described Polish-Ukrainian relations negatively and only 12 per cent positively, the worst result recorded by CBOS. Sixty-five per cent placed greater responsibility for the poor relationship on Ukraine. A majority, 53 per cent, still believed reconciliation was possible, although that too was the lowest level in the history of the survey. This offers Poland’s nationalist right a potent political combination: contemporary migration, welfare, sovereignty and unresolved historical trauma. During the 2025 presidential campaign, anti-Ukrainian messaging became increasingly normalised. Politicians competed over restrictions on benefits and Ukrainian privileges. Grzegorz Braun transformed hostility towards Ukrainian symbols into political theatre. In 2026, leading political figures began linking the Volhynia dispute directly to military and diplomatic relations. This does not establish a causal line from a politician’s speech to an assault on a Ukrainian teenager. It changes the social environment in which such violence occurs. Jacek Kucharczyk, president of Poland’s Institute of Public Affairs, told Rzeczpospolita that a toxic atmosphere generated in politics and online had begun moving into the physical world, producing what he described as an “effect of permission”. The distinction between political hostility and personal violence becomes important precisely when the taboo against aggression starts weakening. The Russian Paradox: Poland Does not Have to Become Pro-Russian Even as Polish attitudes towards Ukrainians sour, attitudes towards Russians remain overwhelmingly negative. CBOS found in February 2026 that 74 per cent of Poles expressed antipathy towards Russians, the highest figure recorded for any nationality in the survey. Attitudes towards Ukrainians have deteriorated for three successive years, while Russia remains deeply unpopular. That apparent contradiction is central to understanding Russian influence operations in Poland. Moscow does not need Poles to become Russophiles. It needs enough Poles to become hostile towards Ukrainians. A Polish voter can regard Vladimir Putin as an enemy, support NATO membership, favour a strong Polish army and simultaneously conclude that Ukraine is exploiting Poland, dishonouring Polish victims, taking Polish welfare money and refusing to reciprocate Polish military assistance. From Moscow’s perspective, that combination works perfectly well. It weakens Polish support for Ukraine while leaving Russia’s disastrous reputation in Poland untouched. Russian information operations therefore have a strong incentive to present themselves in Polish nationalist language rather than overtly Russian language. Their most effective messages start with grievances that already exist. Hard Evidence of Russian Amplification The evidence here is significantly stronger than speculation about individual street attackers. The Institute for Strategic Dialogue documented a coordinated Russia-aligned campaign during Poland’s 2025 presidential election. Operation Overload, also known as Matryoshka, distributed fabricated material claiming that Ukrainian refugees were preparing terrorist attacks during the Polish election. Seven identified X posts accumulated more than 654,000 views. Similar material falsely claimed that Ukrainians planned assassinations of politicians elsewhere in Europe. The operation impersonated established European media organisations and used AI-generated audio. Russia-linked Pravda or Portal Kombat websites spread claims that Ukrainians were responsible for rising Polish crime. Coordinated accounts amplified material portraying Ukrainian refugees as welfare cheats and called for deportations. Polish researchers have recorded the scale of the wider ecosystem. Demagog and the Institute of Media Monitoring identified about 94,000 anti-Ukrainian online posts between April and July 2025, with a potential reach exceeding 32 million contacts. The volume increased substantially later in the year. Rzeczpospolita cites the same research in tracing the connection between electoral politics and the acceleration of anti-Ukrainian content. By summer 2026, Poland’s own state institutions were warning publicly about the mechanism. The Polish Institute of International Affairs, PISM, concluded in August that Russia was the principal beneficiary of the worsening Polish-Ukrainian relationship. Its researchers found that Polish-language references containing extreme anti-Ukrainian hate terminology increased by 171 per cent between 26 May and 13 July, to 364,000 mentions. Engagement with such content rose by 345 per cent. Russian platforms and the Pravda or Portal Kombat network were prominent in the ecosystem. PISM does not claim that Russia created the current dispute but exploited it. The Real Polish Trauma of Volhynia is Valuable to Moscow Russian influence operations become easiest to dismiss when every uncomfortable Polish grievance is labelled “Russian propaganda”. But Volhynia did happen and its victims were real. Polish demands for exhumations and historical acknowledgement have a legitimate basis. Ukrainians themselves have difficult debates over OUN and UPA memory. The Kremlin’s opportunity comes from taking that real wound and manipulating its political meaning. In July, Poland’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs-backed Council of Resilience issued an unusually explicit warning after Russia’s FSB released supposedly newly uncovered materials concerning Volhynia. Polish historians questioned the presentation of those documents. The Council concluded that the Russian operation was attempting to transfer historical emotion into present Polish-Ukrainian relations and ultimately destroy cooperation between the two countries. PISM describes a much longer record: Since at least 2014, according to the institute, Russian actors have exploited unresolved historical questions between Poland and Ukraine. It points to anti-Ukrainian demonstrations, vandalism of memorials, provocations in western Ukraine and attacks on Polish diplomatic premises in the years before the full-scale invasion. Since 2022, the emphasis has increasingly moved towards refugees, welfare, Ukrainian businesses and military support. The tactic is strategically sophisticated because Moscow does not need to falsify the existence of the original grievance. It needs to maximise its emotional intensity, remove context, attach new grievances to it and persuade audiences that a historical crime committed eight decades ago should determine Poland’s strategic relationship with a country currently fighting Russia. Russian Interference has Moved Physical provocation The strongest evidence that this is more than an online problem comes from Poland’s own Internal Security Agency, ABW. In July 2026, Polish prosecutors indicted an 18-year-old Ukrainian citizen, Illia K., alleging that he had carried out sabotage and subversion tasks on the orders of Russian special services. According to the ABW, the purpose was explicitly to inflame national tensions between Poland and Ukraine. Investigators linked him to 47 criminal acts committed between November 2024 and August 2025, including desecration of memorial sites associated with Polish victims of the UPA. He was also accused of preparing sabotage involving an unmanned aircraft. Recruitment took place through internet messaging services and payments were made in cryptocurrency, according to the agency. The alleged Russian operation used a Ukrainian national to conduct anti-Ukrainian provocations involving Polish historical memory. That is almost a textbook example of hybrid influence. The identity of the operative becomes part of the camouflage. An act can appear to confirm an existing ethnic narrative while the strategic beneficiary sits elsewhere. Poland has separately uncovered networks accused of arson, transport sabotage, reconnaissance and other operations carried out for Russian intelligence. Russian services have repeatedly recruited low-level operatives through Telegram and similar platforms, often using money rather than ideology as the incentive. This changes the evidential threshold surrounding the present crisis. There is still no basis for describing every man who punches a Ukrainian in Wrocław or abuses a Ukrainian child on a bus as a Russian agent. Most such violence is far more likely to arise from domestic prejudice, criminal aggression or political radicalisation. There is, however, solid evidence that Russian state actors actively seek to produce, imitate, amplify and exploit Polish-Ukrainian hostility, and that they have commissioned physical provocations designed specifically to deepen it. Moscow’s Most Useful Operation May Require No Russian Operative at All PISM has warned that Russian activity is increasingly concerned with moving “beyond platforms”, encouraging activity in the physical world. The institute assesses that Russia publicises, and may attempt to organise, violent acts against Ukrainians and can use “one-time agents” for vandalism, attacks on activists, destruction of Ukrainian property and other provocations. It also warns of astroturfing, where organised agitation is presented as spontaneous popular mobilisation. A hybrid operation reaches its most effective stage when an adversary no longer needs to manufacture every act itself. Once a hostile narrative has entered domestic political competition, authentic users reproduce it, algorithms reward it, politicians discover votes in it and violent individuals act on it for their own reasons. The foreign operation then needs only to amplify. That is much cheaper, harder to attribute and politically more destructive than conventional propaganda. Poland’s Defence Industry is Entering the Danger Zone This domestic shift also has implications that go well beyond migration policy. Poland has been trying to turn its geographical position, enormous defence budget and proximity to the Ukrainian battlefield into an industrial advantage. Since 2022, Ukrainian defence companies have relocated parts of their activity into EU and NATO territory, including Poland and other Central European states. Polish companies have entered partnerships with Ukrainian producers, while Warsaw and Kyiv have discussed joint ammunition production, unmanned systems, repair, maintenance and technology transfers. OSW, Poland’s Centre for Eastern Studies, reported in April that cooperation intensified after the full-scale invasion as Ukrainian defence companies moved activity into safer EU and NATO jurisdictions. At least several dozen Polish and Ukrainian companies have been involved in cooperation since 2022. The intended model increasingly involves Ukrainian technological and battlefield expertise combined with European capital, production capacity and physical security. For Poland, this has been commercially beneficial. Its armed forces are expanding rapidly. Defence expenditure is around 4.7 per cent of GDP in 2026. Domestic and Central European defence procurement has increased sharply. Companies including Rheinmetall, CSG and other European manufacturers are expanding production or cooperation in Poland. Polish procurement from domestic companies and joint ventures had risen almost fourfold since 2022 to PLN 30.4 billion (EUR 6.9 billion) in 2025. Ukraine adds another layer to that opportunity. Its defence sector has accumulated battlefield knowledge in drones, electronic warfare, target acquisition, software and rapid product iteration that European companies urgently want. Poland has geography, NATO protection, industrial infrastructure, engineers and access to the European market. In theory, this makes it an obvious location for joint Ukrainian-European production. In practice, politics is beginning to interfere. The First Warning: Industrial Cooperation Entangled with the Political Dispute The Polish Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz accused Ukraine of failing to deliver drone technology that he said had previously been promised (Screen Capture / Videoparliament). OSW observed in April that Polish-Ukrainian intergovernmental agreements concluded around the turn of 2025 and 2026 to expand defence-industrial cooperation under the Build with Ukraine programme had still not been implemented. Then came a much more public dispute. In July 2026, Polish Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz accused Ukraine of failing to deliver drone technology that he said had previously been promised in connection with discussions over Poland transferring its remaining MiG-29 aircraft. He explicitly linked the failure to worsening historical tensions, arguing that Kyiv was allowing the history dispute to interfere with cooperation. Ukraine’s position on the alleged agreement was not independently established in the report, so his accusation should be treated as the Polish minister’s account rather than a proven breach by Kyiv. A dispute that had once concerned historical memory had moved directly into defence technology transfer. For investors, these kind of boundaries matter. A joint drone factory, ammunition line or electronic-warfare venture can survive political disagreement. It becomes harder to finance when technology transfer, licensing, government approvals and procurement commitments begin moving with the political relationship. The Second Warning: Physical Security On 31 August, a fire struck a WB Electronics facility at Skarżysko-Kamienna. Polish prosecutors say the fire was deliberately started by placing a device containing flammable material at the facility. Warehousing was destroyed and damage was estimated at least PLN 15 million (EUR 3.4 million). The National Prosecutor’s Office opened its investigation under provisions covering participation in foreign-intelligence activity against Poland and a terrorist offence. The ABW is investigating jointly with prosecutors and police. As of the available public information, nobody has been charged and the foreign state potentially responsible has not been officially identified. Even though there is little direct evidence of that Russia ordered the WB Electronics fire, the incident is strategically serious. WB Electronics is one of Poland’s most important private defence groups. Its unmanned systems have been supplied to and used by Ukraine. The facility therefore sits almost exactly at the intersection that hostile Russian operations would have an interest in targeting: Polish defence production, Ukrainian military capability and expanding European industrial support for Kyiv. Poland has already attributed other major sabotage activity to Russian intelligence, including previous arson and infrastructure plots. The Skarżysko-Kamienna investigation therefore cannot be treated by defence investors as an ordinary industrial fire while a foreign-intelligence inquiry remains open. Now, this is political risk becoming physical risk. Anti-Ukrainian Violence is Already Deterring Defence Investments According to several NDR sources, many Ukraine-linked defence companies are reluctant to establish operations in Poland because of increasingly hostile attitudes towards Ukrainians. For a Ukrainian company considering relocating intellectual property, engineers or production into Poland, the calculation now includes indeed several additional questions. Can Ukrainian technical staff and their families live safely and comfortably in the location chosen for the plant? Can a company recruit Ukrainians without making its workforce a political target? Could a municipal dispute over a Ukrainian-linked facility become attached to nationalist politics? Will a future Polish government alter procurement priorities or cooperation rules as anti-Ukrainian politics becomes electorally profitable? Will security requirements for a Ukrainian-linked plant raise capital expenditure and insurance costs? Could Russian intelligence use employees, subcontractors or low-level recruited operatives to sabotage the venture? For a Western company choosing between Poland, Germany, Denmark, the Czech Republic or another NATO jurisdiction for cooperation with Ukrainian technology, these questions matter, too. Investment decisions depend heavily on predictability. Poland still possesses formidable advantages. It has one of Europe’s largest defence markets, NATO protection, proximity to Ukraine, strong industrial capabilities and an explicit policy of attracting manufacturing and technology transfer. The broader Polish defence-investment boom continues. Rheinmetall and other European companies are expanding activity there. The specific vulnerability is Ukraine-facing investment. Political hostility towards Ukrainians can increase personnel risk. Bilateral disputes can impede technology transfer. Russian sabotage raises site-security costs. A nationalist political backlash can create uncertainty over government policy towards joint Ukrainian production. Each risk reinforces the others. Poland is Valuable to Moscow Because it is Valuable to Ukraine Russia has a strategic reason to concentrate effort on Poland. Poland is one of the principal logistical arteries connecting Ukraine to NATO economies. It is a transit state for military assistance. It trains Ukrainian personnel. Its companies repair and manufacture military equipment. Its territory can host production that would be exposed to Russian missile and drone attack if located inside Ukraine. A Ukrainian defence company moving production from Kyiv or Dnipro to NATO country Poland deprives Russia of one of its advantages: the ability to attack the factory conventionally. That makes Polish territory part of the defence-industrial battlefield. The tools available to Moscow change accordingly. Inside Ukraine, Russia can use missiles and drones. Inside Poland, it needs intelligence operations, sabotage, cyberattacks, political pressure, disinformation and social disruption. Seen from that perspective, anti-Ukrainian agitation is connected to defence industry through strategy rather than through a simplistic conspiracy in which Moscow controls every extremist. If Polish voters become less willing to support Ukraine, military assistance becomes politically costlier. If Ukrainians become socially unwelcome, relocating skilled defence workers becomes harder. If Warsaw and Kyiv become trapped in historical disputes, joint ventures and technology transfers slow down. If factories working for Ukraine require extensive counter-intelligence and physical protection, projects become more expensive. If violence or sabotage gives multinational companies doubts about concentrating Ukraine-related production in Poland, competing European locations gain an advantage. Russia gains something from every stage. Poland’s Difficult Strategic Challenge Warsaw cannot answer the problem by suppressing the Volhynia debate. Polish historical grievances deserve serious treatment. Ukrainian glorification of individuals or organisations responsible for atrocities against Poles inevitably produces political consequences. A democratic Poland will continue debating welfare policy, migration, Ukrainian behaviour and the terms of military assistance. The security task is to prevent those arguments from being transformed into collective hostility towards Ukrainians living in Poland. That requires recognising a distinction Russia works constantly to erase. The Polish prosecutors are pursuing more hate-crime cases and the ABW is exposing Russian recruitment operations. The Polish foreign ministry is openly warning that Russia weaponises Volhynia and Polish researchers are mapping the online networks through which anti-Ukrainian narratives move. But the political system faces the more difficult test. Moscow Only Needs Poland and Ukraine to Hate Each Other Four years after the invasion, Russia has failed spectacularly to make itself attractive to Polish society. Three quarters of Poles still express antipathy towards Russians. The Kremlin can achieve important objectives without changing that figure. A Poland that fears Russia while distrusting Ukraine is strategically more useful to Moscow than a Poland that fears Russia and regards Ukraine as an indispensable partner. A Poland in which the Volhynia massacres are remembered responsibly presents little advantage to the Kremlin. A Poland in which that memory becomes a reason to assault Ukrainians, block military cooperation or abandon joint defence projects presents an opportunity. And a Poland in which domestic actors perform much of that work themselves is the most valuable outcome of all. The recent attacks on Ukrainians should therefore be understood as more than a minority-protection issue. They are becoming a Polish national-security issue. If anti-Ukrainian politics continues moving from social media into the street, and from the street into industrial and defence policy, the strategic beneficiary is already clear. It is the country that Poland itself still regards as its greatest threat. Europe’s Ukraine Consensus is Becoming More Conditional Float with cartoon images of Putin and AfD party leader Alice Weidel and inscription AfD traitors on Rosenmontag parade. Political satire at carnival in Dusseldorf, North Rhine-Westphalia, Germany, February 16, 2026 (Image: Shutterstock) The Polish case belongs to a wider European shift, although the nature of that shift differs sharply from one country to another. There is still little evidence of a general European conversion to sympathy for Vladimir Putin. The European Commission’s spring 2026 Eurobarometer found that 76 per cent of Europeans regarded Russia’s invasion as a threat to EU security, while 81 per cent supported a common European defence and security policy. ECFR polling across 15 European countries in May found that majorities in most countries still regarded Ukraine as either an ally or a necessary strategic partner. What is changing is the willingness to translate that sympathy into open-ended military, financial and social commitments. The four-year emergency has become normal politics. Refugee assistance competes with housing and welfare. Arms deliveries compete with domestic expenditure. Ukrainian EU membership raises questions about agriculture, budgets and minority rights. Fear of Russian escalation coexists with fear that abandoning Ukraine would make Europe less secure. This creates a political environment remarkably well suited to Russian influence operations. Moscow does not need a European majority to endorse Russia’s war. A weaker objective is sufficient: persuade different national audiences that Ukraine is expensive, ungrateful, corrupt, historically objectionable or strategically doomed. The resulting political coalition can contain nationalists, pacifists, anti-establishment voters, fiscal conservatives and parts of the radical left without requiring them to agree on Russia itself. Eastern Germany: Opposition to Ukraine Aid is a Regional Political Identity In eastern Germany, attitudes towards supporting Ukraine are deeply divided. An ARD DeutschlandTrend survey conducted between 31 August and 2 September 2026 found that 54 per cent of respondents in eastern Germany considered German weapons deliveries to Ukraine excessive, compared with 39 per cent in western Germany. Only 42 per cent of eastern Germans regarded Russia as a strong or very strong threat to German security, compared with 59 per cent in the west. Nationally, support for weapons deliveries still narrowly outweighed opposition: 38 per cent considered existing deliveries appropriate and 14 per cent wanted more, while 42 per cent considered them excessive. This east-west difference now has direct electoral consequences. The far-right Alternative für Deutschland party (AfD) has made opposition to sanctions, scepticism towards weapons deliveries and renewed economic relations with Russia important parts of its appeal in the eastern Länder. The September 2026 elections demonstrated how politically powerful that combination has become. AfD won Sachsen-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, while the BSW has also campaigned heavily against sanctions and escalation with Russia. A BSW leader in Sachsen-Anhalt explicitly identified Russia policy as one of the areas in which his party shared positions with the AfD. The AfD’s connections with Russia are extensive and openly cultivated. Co-leader Tino Chrupalla met Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov in Moscow in 2020, AfD politicians have repeatedly visited Russia and attended events at the Russian embassy, and party politicians travelled to Russia as unofficial observers during Putin’s tightly controlled 2024 presidential election. In 2025, an internal dispute erupted over another AfD delegation planning to travel to Sochi and meet senior Russian figures. AfD politician Petr Bystron remains under investigation over suspected payments connected with the pro-Russian Voice of Europe influence network. The European Parliament waived his immunity after German prosecutors alleged that he may have received cash or cryptocurrency in return for speaking and voting in ways beneficial to the Russian government. Bystron denies the allegations, and the case remains unresolved. He and former AfD lead European candidate Maximilian Krah had also maintained contacts with Viktor Medvedchuk, Putin’s long-time Ukrainian ally. The relationship remains current. In September 2026, reports emerged that AfD leaders Alice Weidel and Chrupalla were preparing a meeting with Kirill Dmitriev, one of Putin’s senior economic representatives , to discuss restoring Russian gas supplies to Germany. The Kremlin publicly welcomed the AfD’s desire for dialogue. The AfD simultaneously opposes sanctions and much of Germany’s military assistance to Ukraine. On the German left, the picture again requires a distinction between direct Russian connections and political convergence. The clearest current case is the Bündnis Sahra Wagenknecht, BSW . Wagenknecht and leading party figures oppose arms deliveries and sanctions and favour the restoration of Russian energy imports. ARD’s Faktenfinder has documented several instances in which BSW politicians circulated claims about Ukraine that closely followed Kremlin narratives, including claims subsequently shown to be false. A BSW MP’s employee was separately revealed by Correctiv to have appeared at an event involving Russian ultranationalist ideologue Alexander Dugin. The contacts are also overt. In 2025, the BSW parliamentary group in Brandenburg invited Russian ambassador Sergei Nechayev into the state parliament. In September 2026, after the Sachsen-Anhalt election, BSW politicians identified Russia policy, opposition to sanctions and energy relations as areas of agreement with the AfD, and the two parties entered talks in which “peace policy” was explicitly on the agenda. Germany therefore demonstrates something particularly important for the wider European argument. Russia does not need a single ideological proxy. The AfD approaches the issue through nationalism, sovereignty, energy and hostility towards the existing European order. The BSW approaches it through anti-Americanism, economic opposition to sanctions and hostility towards military escalation. Their politics differ considerably elsewhere. On Russia, sanctions and weapons for Ukraine, they can arrive at remarkably similar positions. That helps explain why eastern Germany is so different from Poland. Polish anti-Ukrainian sentiment can coexist with profound hostility towards Russia. In Germany, particularly in the east, resistance to supporting Ukraine is much more closely connected with a positive argument for restoring relations with Moscow itself. The common argument of both German far-right and far-left concerns the war itself: sanctions hurt Germans, weapons prolong the conflict, diplomacy requires accommodation with Moscow and domestic spending should take priority. A domestic grievance becomes more politically effective when Ukraine is made responsible for it. Poland’s deterioration has increasingly involved Ukrainians living in the country. In eastern Germany, resistance to aiding Ukraine appears to be driven more by opposition to military support and scepticism about confrontation with Russia than by strong hostility towards Ukrainian refugees, still less by anti-Ukrainian street violence. Czechia: A More Complicated Course At the 80th United Nations General Assembly (UNGA80) in New York, President Petr Pavel of Czechia condemned the deportation of Ukrainian children under Russian occupation as a grave violation of international law and humanity. (Screen Capture / Eurodebates) The Czech Republic shows the difference between campaign rhetoric and government. Before the 2025 election, Andrej Babiš said a government led by ANO would stop Czech weapons deliveries to Ukraine. His eventual government has taken a more complicated course. The Czech ammunition initiative has survived, although Prague has sought to reduce direct Czech financial exposure and rely increasingly on foreign contributors. President Petr Pavel said in May that the number of countries financing the initiative had fallen from 18 to nine. The contradiction became especially visible in July 2026. The Czech government agreed to make a contribution to the NATO-led PURL mechanism for purchasing American weaponry for Ukraine. Prime Minister Babiš described the payment as small and one-off. Foreign Minister Petr Macinka called it essentially symbolic. The SPD, Babiš’s coalition partner, opposed even that contribution. Czech media subsequently reported that approximately CZK 140 million (EUR 5.7 million) had been transferred. Yet Babiš himself has simultaneously hardened his language about Russia. In September 2026 he publicly said that Russia was conducting hybrid warfare against the Czech Republic, causing irritation among SPD politicians who continued advocating imports of cheap Russian energy. Czech policy has therefore become more conditional, cheaper for the Czech taxpayer and politically more contentious. It has not become straightforwardly aligned with Moscow. The Czech defence industry has become one of the economic beneficiaries of European rearmament and the war in Ukraine. Babiš’s own government contains politicians who regard defence production as an important source of Czech industrial growth. That creates a powerful material counterweight to anti-aid politics. The Czech case may therefore become a model for a broader European compromise: rhetorical distance from Kyiv, limits on taxpayer-funded aid, continued commercial weapons production and continued participation in selected NATO mechanisms. Slovakia: the Anti-aid Position has Moved into Government Policy Slovakia has gone further than the Czech Republic. Prime Minister Robert Fico returned to office on an explicit promise to end state military assistance to Ukraine. His rhetoric has subsequently moved beyond budgetary scepticism into a broader argument that Western governments are prolonging the conflict and increasing the danger of a direct NATO-Russia war. On 19 September 2026, Fico argued that some Western politicians were effectively seeking a confrontation between Russia and NATO. Slovak media have repeatedly documented the same political theme: the war is presented as something Slovakia should keep at maximum distance, and Western military support is portrayed as a potential route towards escalation. These arguments fall on unusually fertile ground. GLOBSEC’s multi-year surveys have consistently shown Slovakia among the Central and Eastern European countries with the greatest scepticism towards military support for Ukraine and some of the strongest receptiveness to narratives that place responsibility for escalation on NATO or the West. The divergence predates Fico’s current government. His political success has institutionalised it. Slovakia therefore differs from Poland in a fundamental way. Poland’s government remains strategically committed to Ukrainian survival despite deteriorating public opinion. Fico’s government has incorporated scepticism towards military support directly into state policy. For Russian strategy, this is the more direct prize. title: Danish intelligence warns Russia could attack NATO
body: Denmark’s military intelligence service says there is a low but growing risk that Russia could carry out a limited military attack against one or more NATO countries bordering Russia, potentially within the coming months and even while the war in Ukraine continues. In a new unclassified assessment of the threat from Russia , the Danish Defence Intelligence Service said Moscow had become more willing to take risks and was expected to intensify its hybrid campaign against NATO and the West. The service pointed to sabotage, destructive cyber attacks and drone activity in Europe, while saying Russian forces had also behaved increasingly aggressively towards NATO military units in the Baltic Sea region. The assessment said: “There is a low but growing risk that Russia will launch a limited military attack against one or several NATO countries bordering Russia. This could happen even if Russia continues the war against Ukraine and has not built the military capabilities necessary to wage a regional war.” Danish intelligence said such an attack would be a “desperate move” and could be intended to divert European resources away from Ukraine or create divisions within NATO over how the Alliance should respond. One scenario set out in the assessment involves isolated long-range strikes against infrastructure used to support Ukraine, followed by a Russian claim that weapons entered NATO territory because of Ukrainian jamming. Another possibility identified by the service is a false-flag attack using Ukrainian-made drones. The assessment also considers the possibility of Russia deploying a small number of troops, potentially without national insignia, into a NATO country bordering Russia. Danish intelligence said such an operation would probably be preceded by a build-up of regular Russian forces near the border to prepare for a possible NATO response, a process it assessed would take several months and be difficult to conceal. At the same time, the service said it had seen no indications that Russia was preparing an outright invasion of a NATO country and judged such an attack to be highly unlikely. It estimated that Moscow would need at least six months to prepare and assemble the forces necessary for an invasion, while warning that the possibility could no longer be completely ruled out. The report said Russia would probably contemplate limited military action only if Moscow believed it would not trigger a collective NATO military response. It added that Russia was likely uncertain about where that threshold lies, particularly if it assessed that the United States could not or would not support European NATO members in a conflict. Danish intelligence also expects Russia to increase the frequency and severity of hybrid attacks against Western countries. It said recent Russian activity had increasingly moved beyond attempts to create fear or reduce public support for Ukraine and towards directly interfering with military assistance, including sabotage against defence companies and railway transport carrying military equipment. The service said future activity could include destructive cyber attacks capable of disabling critical public functions and sabotage carrying a high risk of casualties. It also cited a warning by Denmark’s domestic security service that Russia was planning and preparing sabotage against defence companies on Danish territory. The updated assessment retains timelines published by Danish intelligence in February 2025 under a separate set of assumptions, including an end or freezing of the war in Ukraine, continued Russian military expansion and insufficient Western rearmament. Under those conditions, the service assessed that Russia could be capable of fighting a local war against a neighbouring country within around six months, pose a credible regional threat to several Baltic NATO members within two years and be ready for a large-scale European war within around five years. Danish Foreign Minister Lars Løkke Rasmussen described the assessment as “deeply concerning”, saying: “Russia will escalate hybrid attacks, and low but increasing risk of limited attacks against NATO countries. We will not let ourselves be intimidated, but will continue support for Ukraine, pressure on Russia, and European rearmament.” The post Danish intelligence warns Russia could attack NATO first appeared on UK Defence Journal .
